skill.name: IoT UART Console (picocom)
skill.description: Use picocom and a Python serial helper to connect to authorized IoT UART consoles, log sessions, send commands, and document security observations.
skill.summary: Connect to authorized IoT UART consoles with picocom and scripted serial logging.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: The helper script is mostly standard serial-console automation, but the documentation contains confirmed high-risk dual-use content. Confirmed findings include authentication bypass, privilege escalation, password and key discovery, firmware extraction, network scanning, and persistence guidance.

remediation.issue: Backdoor and persistence instructions are included in the main guide and examples.
remediation.suggestion: Remove commands that create UID 0 users, install SSH keys, add startup entries, or create reverse shells. Replace them with defensive verification checks only.

remediation.issue: Authentication bypass and root-shell workflows are presented as operational steps.
remediation.suggestion: Limit bootloader guidance to documenting exposure and remediation. Avoid instructions that modify bootargs to bypass login.

remediation.issue: Firmware dumps and netcat transfer examples can exfiltrate device contents.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit authorization, use local-only evidence handling, and avoid external transfer examples in marketplace-facing content.

remediation.issue: Session logs are stored in predictable /tmp paths and may contain secrets.
remediation.suggestion: Use a private directory with restrictive permissions and warn users before logging credentials, keys, or tokens.

remediation.issue: Sudo and destructive device commands are shown without confirmation gates.
remediation.suggestion: Add explicit user confirmation before privileged commands, process killing, flash reads, or writes to system paths.

content.user_title: Inspect IoT UART Consoles with Picocom
content.value_statement: IoT UART testing is slow when serial sessions are hard to observe and document. This skill provides guided picocom workflows, helper-script commands, and logging practices for authorized device work.
actual_capabilities: Connects to serial devices such as /dev/ttyUSB0 and /dev/ttyACM0.
Uses picocom or the included Python helper for command-based serial interaction.
Supports session logging so users can observe serial input and output.
Provides baud rate, prompt, timeout, raw output, and JSON output options.
Guides authorized enumeration of embedded Linux and U-Boot console states.
limitations: Requires physical UART access and the correct serial adapter wiring.
Requires picocom or pyserial to be installed before use.
Cannot validate device ownership or authorization by itself.
Unsafe commands can damage devices or expose sensitive data if used carelessly.

use_cases.title: Document an authorized hardware test
use_cases.description: Connect to a lab device, capture the UART session, and record basic system observations.

use_cases.title: Debug serial console behavior
use_cases.description: Try baud rates, detect prompts, and compare raw and cleaned serial output during device bring-up.

use_cases.title: Review bootloader exposure
use_cases.description: Observe boot messages and document whether a bootloader console is exposed on an approved target.

prompt_templates.title: Start a logged UART session
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for an authorized device.
prompt_templates.prompt: Connect to my authorized device on /dev/ttyUSB0 at 115200 baud and log the UART session for observation.

prompt_templates.title: Enumerate basic device state
prompt_templates.scenario: Collect safe context from a known prompt.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the serial helper to run basic read-only checks on my authorized IoT device and summarize the findings.

prompt_templates.title: Troubleshoot console output
prompt_templates.scenario: Resolve garbled output or missing prompts.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me diagnose a UART session with garbled output. Try common baud rates and explain the likely cause.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a test report outline
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced reporting after an approved assessment.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the logged serial session from my authorized assessment and create a concise findings outline with evidence notes.

output_examples.input: Connect to /dev/ttyUSB0 and show whether the prompt is ready.
output_examples.output: The session connected at 115200 baud. A shell-style prompt was detected, and the log file captured the interaction.
The device exposed a serial console, reported an embedded Linux environment, and showed network configuration details.
The symptoms match an incorrect baud rate. Test the common rates and keep the wiring unchanged during comparison.

best_practices: Use the skill only on devices you own or have explicit permission to test.
Store session logs in a protected directory because they can contain secrets.
Prefer read-only enumeration before making any device or bootloader changes.
anti_patterns: Do not use default credentials against devices without authorization.
Do not add persistence, users, keys, or startup commands to production devices.
Do not place sensitive UART logs in shared temporary directories.

faq.question: What does this skill need before it can run?
faq.answer: It needs a UART adapter, a serial device path, and picocom or pyserial installed.

faq.question: Can it work with Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. The report declares support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it require root access?
faq.answer: Serial access may require device permissions or group membership. Some optional monitoring methods use sudo.

faq.question: Can logs contain sensitive data?
faq.answer: Yes. UART logs can include passwords, keys, tokens, network data, and device identifiers.

faq.question: Is this safe for unmanaged third-party devices?
faq.answer: No. Use it only for authorized testing on devices you own or are approved to assess.

faq.question: What is the safest workflow?
faq.answer: Start with a logged read-only session, document observations, and avoid modifying boot or account settings.
